title: Signatures Set the Price
goal: Every parameter and return type decides what your callers must pay.

sections.text: This deck is different: several answers compile and pass the tests. The question is which signature treats the caller best. A function's types are its pricing policy. A `String` parameter demands ownership, so a caller who wants to keep their value must clone it. A `&str` parameter costs every caller nothing: owned strings coerce, and literals just work.

sections.caption: The cheapest parameter type serves every caller.

sections.text: Return types follow the same logic. Returning `&str` hands back a view into data the caller already owns: zero allocation, and lifetime elision ties it to the input. Returning `String` allocates, which is the honest choice when the function builds new data. Returning by mutating a `&mut` parameter is the most invasive shape: it forces `mut` into the caller's code.

The general rule: accept the most flexible type that the body can work with, usually `&str` over `&String` and `&[T]` over `&Vec<T>`. Return views when the data already exists, owned values when you created something new. Reach for `&mut` parameters only when measurement says the allocation matters.

explanation: Parameter and return types are the price you charge callers. Accept flexible views, return owned data only when you built it.
